children.value: The previous sections traced a progression from BM25 through LSI and word embeddings to transformer-based models. At each step, we reduced the independence assumption between tokens, gaining recall: documents that share no surface terms with the query can now be retrieved through semantic similarity. But this gain comes at three costs that classical retrieval did not face:

Dense vectors cannot use inverted indices. Comparing a query against one million document embeddings requires one million dot products. We examine vector search acceleration in the next chapter, but no method matches the pruning efficiency of inverted files for sparse vectors.

Casting a wider semantic net retrieves more relevant documents, but also more noise. A query for “training large language models” will match papers about “optimizing neural networks” (relevant) and “training dogs with reinforcement signals” (not relevant). Cross-encoders (see
) address this through reranking, but at the cost of a full transformer forward pass per candidate.

Encoding a multi-page document into a single 768-dimensional vector discards detail. Chunking the document into shorter passages mitigates this, but multiplies the number of vectors to store and search.
Every design decision in a semantic search pipeline is a tradeoff among three dimensions:

(precision and recall for the use case). There is no single optimal pipeline. A factual search engine serving millions of short queries per second operates in a different region of this space than a patent lawyer who needs exhaustive recall and is willing to wait for a thorough assessment.
This section shows how to navigate these tradeoffs through pipeline design, model selection, and efficiency techniques.
Before designing a pipeline, we need to choose the embedding model that will produce the dense vectors. The

These numbers are approximate and hardware-dependent, but the ratios are instructive: BM25 is orders of magnitude faster than dense search, and cross-encoder reranking is orders of magnitude slower than retrieval. This cost structure drives the pipeline architectures below. The hands-on notebook for this section benchmarks these pipelines on a 500-movie collection and compares a small and a larger embedding model on ranking quality and cost (latency and storage), making these tradeoffs concrete.

is the baseline from classical retrieval: an inverted index with BM25 scoring, no semantic component. It is fast, well-understood, and sufficient when queries and documents share vocabulary. The subsequent pipelines add semantic components to address its limitations.

This works well when BM25 recall is sufficient: if the relevant documents contain at least some of the query terms, BM25 will find them, and the cross-encoder improves the ordering. It fails when the vocabulary mismatch is severe. All three pipelines require splitting long documents into shorter passages. The optimal chunk size differs by component:

tolerates large chunks (full sections, even full documents). It scores individual terms within the chunk; surrounding irrelevant text does not affect the score of matching terms. Traditional retrieval systems typically chunk at the page or section level.

need shorter chunks (256-1024 tokens). The entire chunk is compressed into a single vector, so irrelevant content dilutes the embedding. Paragraph-level or sliding-window chunking with overlap produces the best results.

can handle longer inputs (up to their context window) because they read query and document jointly with full token interaction. They are typically applied to the chunks retrieved by the earlier stages.

In hybrid systems, a common approach is to chunk at a granularity that works for the bi-encoder (the most sensitive component) and use the same chunks for BM25. The result metadata links chunks back to their source documents so that the final output can present either chunk-level or document-level results. We discuss chunking strategies (fixed-size, recursive, semantic, hierarchical) in detail in the RAG chapter, where the interaction between chunk design and generation quality adds further constraints.
Efficiency at Scale: Multi-Stage Retrieval (Pipeline E)

children.label: Efficiency at Scale: Multi-Stage Retrieval (Pipeline E)

children.value: As collections grow from thousands to millions of documents, the cost of encoding, storing, and searching becomes the dominant concern. Pipeline E addresses this with

: a cheap first stage scans the full collection for fast filtering, then a precise full-precision second stage reranks the surviving candidates. The two subsections below are variants of this pipeline. They differ only in how the cheap first stage is built: Matryoshka embeddings truncate the vector to a low dimension, while binary or scalar quantization compress each dimension into fewer bits.

Traditional embeddings use a fixed number of dimensions. Matryoshka embeddings (Kusupati et al., 2022) train the model so that truncated prefixes of the embedding remain useful: the first 64 dimensions capture coarse semantics, the first 128 add detail, and the full vector provides maximum precision. The training objective adds loss terms at multiple truncation levels:

The second variant of Pipeline E builds the cheap first stage through quantization rather than truncation. A compressed (quantized) index handles the fast filtering over the full collection, then the surviving candidates are rescored with the full-precision embeddings. Storage and comparison costs can be further reduced through quantization:

: replace each float dimension with a single bit (positive to 1, negative to 0). Reduces storage by 32x and enables fast Hamming distance computation. Quality loss is typically 5-10% on retrieval benchmarks.
(int8): map each float to an 8-bit integer. Reduces storage by 4x with minimal quality loss (typically less than 2%).
Quantization is most effective as a first-stage filter: use quantized embeddings for coarse candidate retrieval, then rescore with full-precision embeddings.
There is no single best pipeline. The right design depends on where your application sits in the cost-latency-quality space. The following recommendations serve as starting points, not prescriptions.
Brute-force search is fast enough; no need for BM25 infrastructure or ANN indices
BM25 handles exact match; dense retrieval handles semantic match; cross-encoder refines
Pipeline E (multi-stage: Matryoshka or quantized first stage)
Multi-stage retrieval keeps latency manageable; ANN index required (see next chapter)
Small bi-encoder (33M-137M), short chunks, fast reranker
Large bi-encoder (7B+), hybrid retrieval, aggressive cross-encoder reranking, accept higher latency
Hybrid mandatory (product IDs need BM25); lightweight reranker or no reranker
Multilingual model (BGE-M3, Qwen3), hybrid retrieval, moderate reranking

Dense embeddings create the vectors; Chapter 6 (Vector Search) addresses how to efficiently index and search them at scale using approximate nearest neighbor algorithms (HNSW, IVF, product quantization). Chapter 7 (RAG) builds on the retrieval pipeline by feeding retrieved chunks to a language model for answer generation, adding further constraints on chunk design and result quality.

The notebook also shows the Matryoshka recall-versus-storage curve, and why a small model plus BM25 can nearly match a far more expensive large model.
